transcription.tex: Calculate the value of the following. You may use the factorial button, but not the nCr button.
\text{\(0!=1\). Accept this for now; part (e) explains why.}
\text{There are 20 ways to choose 1 object from 20.}\par\text{ \(\binom{20}1=\frac{20!}{1!19!}=20\). In general, \(\binom n1=n\).}
\text{Choosing no objects is one possible selection.}\par\text{ \(\binom{20}0=\frac{20!}{0!20!}=1\), which requires \(0!=1\). In general, \(\binom n0=1\).}

transcription.tex: \text{For large powers such as \((x+3)^{20}\), building Pascal’s triangle becomes impractical. The choose function gives any entry directly.}

\text{Number the top row 0 and the first entry 0. Entry \(k\) in row \(n\) is \(\binom nk\): the top number gives the row, the bottom number gives the entry.}\par\text{ The textbook starts counting at 1; here we count from 0 so the numbers match the binomial coefficient directly.}
\text{The triangle is symmetric:\[\binom41=\binom43.\]Choosing one object is equivalent to choosing the three objects to leave out.}

transcription.tex: \text{Pascal’s rule: each interior entry is the sum of the two above it.\[\binom31+\binom32=3+3=6=\binom42\]\[\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\binom{n-1}k=\binom nk\]}

\text{To choose k objects from n, focus on one particular object. Either include it and choose k−1 from the other n−1, or exclude it and choose k from the other n−1. These cases are disjoint and cover every selection.}

(b) Coefficient of \(x^3\) is \(120q^3\). Coefficient of \(x\) is \(10q\).\[\begin{aligned}\text{So }120q^3&=108\times10q\\\Rightarrow120q^3-1080q&=0\\\Rightarrow120q(q^2-9)&=0\\\Rightarrow120q(q+3)(q-3)&=0\\q=0,\ q=-3&\text{ or }q=3\end{aligned}\]But as \(q\) is non-zero, \(q=\pm3\).

transcription.tex: A microchip company models the probability of having no faulty chips on a single production run as:\[\mathrm P(\text{no fault})=(1-p)^n,\ p<0.001\]where \(p\) is the probability of a single chip being faulty, and \(n\) being the total number of chips produced.\par (a) State why the model is restricted to small values of \(p\). \par (b) Given that \(n=200\), find an approximate expression for \(\mathrm P(\text{no fault})\) in the form \(a+bp+cp^2\). \par (c) The company wants to achieve a \(92\%\) likelihood of having no faulty chips on a production run of 200 chips. Use your answer to part \textbf{b} to suggest a maximum value of \(p\) for this to be the case.
(a) Small p makes truncation after p² useful for fixed n. The exact independent-chip probability (1−p)ⁿ does not itself require p<0.001.

(c) \[19900p^2-200p+0.08=0\]\[p=\frac{200\pm\sqrt{33632}}{39800}\]The roots are approximately 0.00963 and 0.000417. Only the latter satisfies p<0.001, so the approximate maximum is p=0.000417 (3 s.f.).
